title: Cascading Through the Hierarchy: Regularizer-Induced Feature Detection as Phase Transitions in Deep Linear Neural Networks
authors: Björn Ladewig, Ibrahim Talha Ersoy, Karoline Wiesner
abstract: A scientific theory of deep learning, comprising learning dynamics and statistical properties of learned models, is rapidly gaining attention. One of the corner stones of this development are analytically solvable toy models, allowing for the fully tractable analysis of the learning dynamics. Here we analytically investigate such a toy model using the regularization strength as a tunable external parameter - akin to external fields in statistical physics. In previous studies, (i) an onset of learning transition was predicted analytically and (ii) it was phenomenologically/numerically established that tuning the regularization strength can result in a cascade of phase transitions. The number of those transitions was linked to the geometry of the loss landscape determined by the model complexity. Setting up a rigorous framework underpinning the previous numerical observations, our investigation reveals a precise connection between those cascades of phase transitions, learnable features and the underlying geometry. We provide analytic predictions of these phase transitions as well as tractable order parameters related to learned features. At the level of the minimal model, we connect this macroscopic perspective (that can be condensed into an effective description) to the microscopic perspective in terms of the geometry of the loss landscape characterized by the Hessian spectrum. Thus, the presented model provides a platform to explore and sharpen advances made in the scientific theory of deep learning rooted in statistical physics concepts.
summary: This paper develops a statistical physics framework to understand deep learning by treating the regularization strength as an external field controlling phase transitions. Using analytically solvable linear neural networks, the authors rigorously connect observed feature detection cascades to the underlying geometry of the loss landscape via Hessian spectrum analysis. It provides powerful theoretical tools for interpreting network training dynamics through the lens of critical phenomena.
main_problem: The paper develops a scientific theory of deep learning by connecting its learning dynamics and statistical properties to concepts from statistical physics, specifically investigating how regularization induces phase transitions.
main_result: It establishes a rigorous link between cascades of phase transitions, the learnable features detected by the network, and the underlying geometry characterized by the Hessian spectrum. The analysis provides analytic predictions for these transitions using order parameters derived from an effective free energy description.
method: The authors employ analytical techniques to study analytically solvable toy models (Deep Linear Neural Networks), treating the regularization strength as a tunable external field analogous to statistical physics Hamiltonians.
model_or_system: The system is Deep Linear Neural Networks (DLN) trained with Mean Squared Error loss and $L_2$ weight decay regularization. The analysis focuses on the dynamics of the weights, relating macroscopic behavior to the microscopic geometry of the loss landscape via the Hessian spectrum.
key_observables: Phase transitions, order parameters related to learned features, and the eigenvalues/spectrum of the Jacobian/Hessian matrix.
important_parameters: Regularization strength ($ eta$), network depth ($n$), and data covariance matrices ($\Sigma_{xx}, \Sigma_{yx}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to deep linear models (DLN) and often assumes zero mean for simplicity. The connection between the macroscopic effective description and microscopic Hessian spectrum provides the core theoretical framework.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the qualitative structure of the regularized loss landscape, showing level crossings indicative of first-order transitions, bifurcation points, and examples of the Hessian spectrum across different network depths.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the connection between learning dynamics and statistical physics. It analyzes the critical point structure for DLNs using regularization strength as a control parameter, deriving order parameters from the loss function's effective potential (Landau theory). Finally, it tackles the microscopic details by analyzing the Jacobian/Hessian spectrum to confirm these macroscopic predictions.
why_interesting: The explicit mapping of deep learning phenomena (feature detection) onto established concepts like phase transitions and Hessian spectra provides a powerful theoretical analogy for understanding complex many-body systems or critical points in other physical models.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1: (a) Qualitative summary of the main features of the regularized loss landscape for > 1 hidden layers and small regularization strength; (b) level crossing (marked by dotted vertical lines) at the level of the loss inducing first order transitions; (c) bifurcation (indicated by dashed vertical lines) at the level of the mean squared error; (d) example of the Hessian spectrum for 2 hidden layers. For (b-d): η1 = 0.95, η2 = 0.55, η3 = 0.3.

FIG. 2: Path through the loss landscape, based on Hessian eigendirections revealing a basin structure in the unregularized (β →0) loss landscape for 2 hidden layers featuring one global minimum and multiple saddle points (7) that partly correspond to rank-restricted optima. With: Σxx = 13×3, Σyx = diag(0.95, 0.55, 0.3).

FIG. 3: (a, c) Minimal loss L∗and MSE for 1 hidden layer (top) and 2 hidden layers (bottom). Colored dashed parts correspond to the loss/MSE for a reversed annealing protocol. (b,d) Basin structure in the regularized loss landscape for deep linear networks with 1 hidden layer (top) - featuring one minimum; and 2 hidden layers (bottom) - featuring multiple minima - for different regularization strengths β. Vertical lines indicate critical regularization strengths (in case of 1st order transitions there are two, see main text).

FIG. 4: Effective loss landscapes (1 hidden layer) for η1 = 0.95, η2 = 0.55, η3 = 0.3; the right most plot shows the minima σ∗ i of the effective potentials (16) as a function of β, displaying the continuous onset at critical regularization strengths β∗ i .

FIG. 5: Hessian spectra for 1 hidden (a,b) and 2 hidden layers (c,d) with din = dout = dhidden = 3 and η1 = 0.95, η2 = 0.55, η3 = 0.3 based on numerical simulations (reversed annealing) and analytical prediction: (a) Hessian spectra for 1 hidden layer and different, fixed β: (i) rmax(β) = 0 (square); (ii) rmax(β) = 3 (circle); (b) Hessian spectrum as a function of β. (c) Hessian spectra for 2 hidden layers and different, fixed β for (i) rmax(β) = 0 (diamond), (ii) rmax(β) = 1 (square) and (iii) rmax(β) = rmax (circle); (d) Hessian spectrum as a function of β.
